name: Serratia bacterial leaf spot
summary: A pathogenicity-confirmed Cannabis bacterial disease producing small vein-limited angular lesions that can coalesce across leaves, stems and flower parts. Red bacterial ooze is useful supporting evidence but species confirmation requires laboratory identification.
affectedParts: leaves | stems | flower parts
indicators: Small dark-brown 1–3 mm lesions are angular or vein-limited | Lesions coalesce into larger necrotic regions as disease advances | Red bacterial ooze streams from affected plant tissue | Laboratory culture and 16S/rpoB or equivalent evidence supports Serratia marcescens
exclusions: No bacterial ooze or lab evidence exists and lesions fit a fungal leaf spot better | Xanthomonas or another bacterial pathogen is identified | Chemical/contact injury follows a spray or exposure boundary
lookAlikes: Xanthomonas bacterial leaf spot | Septoria leaf spot | Cercospora leaf spot | Anthracnose | Contact spray injury
confirmation: Collect fresh lesion-margin tissue for bacterial isolation and molecular identification. | Treat red ooze as a strong clue, not a substitute for organism confirmation.
immediateActions: Separate strongly affected propagation material and avoid moving wet symptomatic tissue through clean areas. | Preserve a fresh sample before sanitation.
correctivePlan: Use laboratory-confirmed bacterial-disease sanitation and management appropriate to the production system.
prevention: Sanitize tools/contact surfaces and minimize splash movement from symptomatic plants. | Use clean propagation material.
warnings: Serratia includes strains of human-health relevance; use appropriate hygiene and diagnostic-lab handling. | Angular necrotic lesions alone are not Serratia-specific.

name: Xanthomonas bacterial leaf spot
summary: A documented bacterial leaf spot of hemp in which small water-soaked lesions progress to approximately 1–2 mm necrotic centers surrounded by comparatively broad yellow halos; images can support triage but cannot distinguish the bacterium from fungal or abiotic look-alikes.
affectedParts: leaf blades | upper and lower leaf surfaces
stages: growth stage not established in cannabis-specific primary evidence
indicators: Small water-soaked leaf spots before necrosis develops | Necrotic centers approximately 1–2 mm in diameter | Yellow halos approximately 2–3 mm wide | Discrete lesions with a halo wider than the necrotic center | Focal spotting rather than a whole-leaf nutrient-mobility gradient
exclusions: White surface colonies, fungal fruiting structures, or diagnostic spores support a fungal cause | Fine stippling, webbing, or organisms on the leaf underside support arthropod feeding | Damage follows spray droplets, contact points, or a documented chemical application and does not progress after exposure ends | Symptoms follow a measured older-leaf or younger-leaf nutrient pattern without discrete water-soaked lesions | A plant diagnostic laboratory identifies another pathogen or abiotic cause from a representative active lesion
lookAlikes: Septoria or other fungal leaf spot | Alternaria leaf spot | Cercospora leaf spot | Foliar spray injury | Edema or water-soaking from physiological stress | Thrips or mite feeding punctures | Localized nutrient or salt injury
confirmation: Photograph the whole plant and both sides of several leaves, then capture a scale-referenced close-up showing the necrotic-center and halo dimensions and the distribution of lesions across the canopy. | Submit fresh, recently expanding lesions that include the transition between healthy and affected tissue to a plant diagnostic laboratory; keep samples separate, cool, and dry according to that laboratory’s instructions. | Ask the laboratory to distinguish bacterial from fungal leaf spot and, if a Xanthomonas isolate is recovered, identify it with validated physiological and molecular or sequence-based methods rather than morphology alone. | Microscopic bacterial streaming may support a bacterial differential, but absence of streaming does not exclude bacteria and streaming does not confirm Xanthomonas cannabis to species. | Map reports using the current accepted name Xanthomonas cannabis while retaining Xanthomonas campestris pv. cannabis as a historical synonym for literature and laboratory searches.
immediateActions: Flag the plant and pause movement of cuttings or symptomatic foliage until laboratory triage. | Handle suspect foliage only when dry, avoid splash between plants, and clean hands and tools before moving to unaffected plants. | Keep unconfirmed lesion photographs out of bacterial ground-truth and training sets.
correctivePlan: Base removal, sanitation, and any crop treatment on the confirmed diagnosis and local legal label; a visual bacterial-leaf-spot suspicion is not a treatment prescription. | Inspect nearby plants for comparable small haloed lesions and document whether new lesions appear after splash or handling events without treating that association as proof. | If laboratory results do not recover or identify the bacterium, reopen fungal, arthropod, chemical, and physiological differentials.
prevention: Use documented healthy propagation material and retain lot or mother-plant traceability. | Minimize leaf wetness and splash during routine handling where compatible with the production system. | Disinfect tools and segregate symptomatic material under a written sanitation protocol.
warnings: A photograph or video cannot confirm Xanthomonas cannabis; lesion size and halo geometry are triage features only. | The key symptom measurements come from a historical Japanese hemp report and do not establish current local prevalence, cultivar susceptibility, or production-system risk. | General greenhouse bacterial-leaf-spot guidance is used only for differential diagnosis and handling precautions, not as cannabis-specific epidemiological proof. | No cannabis-specific image or video with verified reuse and automated-training permission was found for this batch; no media was copied or admitted.

name: High-temperature or high-light exposure
summary: Measured high temperature or unusually intense light can alter Cannabis physiology, yield, and flowering development, but published Cannabis experiments do not validate cupping, bleaching, or a single PPFD or temperature value as a universal visible injury diagnosis.
affectedParts: whole canopy | upper and lower inflorescences | recently expanded leaves | canopy nearest a local heat or light source
stages: vegetative | flower initiation | flower development | late flower
indicators: Air temperature, leaf temperature, PPFD, photoperiod, and humidity are recorded at the affected canopy position across time | Abnormal new inflorescence clusters develop on top of older inflorescences during sustained high-temperature flowering exposure | Flower maturation or production differs from a matched cultivar under a cooler measured regime | Gas-exchange or chlorophyll-fluorescence measurements change even when a specific foliar lesion is absent | A spatial gradient repeats with measured temperature or irradiance rather than merely with leaf age
exclusions: No time-stamped canopy-level temperature, leaf-temperature, PPFD, photoperiod, or humidity record supports an exposure event | Only upward leaf curl, pale tissue, dry margins, or canopy posture is visible | Mites, thrips, webbing, cast skins, eggs, frass, or feeding scars are present | Root-zone water content, irrigation history, pH, EC, or root disease explains the distribution better | The change follows nutrient, pesticide, growth-regulator, or other chemical application | Only late-flower senescence or cultivar-typical inflorescence architecture is visible | High PPFD alone is treated as injury even though the plant is acclimated and temperature and water status are within its measured response range
lookAlikes: Water shortage or excessive vapor demand | Potassium deficiency | High root-zone EC or pH-related nutrient unavailability | Hemp russet mite | Broad mite | Thrips injury | Wind or fan injury | Pesticide or plant-growth-regulator injury | Normal late-flower senescence | Cultivar-typical foxtailing or inflorescence architecture
confirmation: Map PPFD and air temperature at multiple canopy positions and times; measure leaf temperature with a calibrated contact or infrared method and record humidity or vapor-pressure deficit, photoperiod, carbon dioxide, and lamp distance. | Compare affected and unaffected plants of the same cultivar, developmental stage, irrigation treatment, and root-zone condition; include a cooler or lower-exposure reference when available. | Inspect leaf undersides and protected new growth with magnification for mites and thrips, and document the root system, substrate water content, pH, and EC. | Use serial whole-plant, canopy, and close-up images with an exposure log; do not convert a single photograph or uncalibrated camera color shift into heat- or light-stress ground truth. | For abnormal flowering, inspect multiple inflorescences over time and compare with cultivar records to separate heat-associated reversion or foxtailing from normal architecture, late-flower growth, or genetic traits.
immediateActions: Preserve the pre-correction environmental log and matched photographs, then remove an acute unsafe heat load or equipment fault gradually. | Verify irrigation delivery and root-zone moisture before changing light, humidity, or irrigation together. | Quarantine or isolate only when pest or infectious disease evidence warrants it; environmental exposure alone is not contagious.
correctivePlan: Correct the measured source, such as a canopy hot spot, failed cooling or air mixing, excessive lamp proximity, or an abrupt unacclimated light increase, while changing one controllable factor at a time. | Re-map the canopy after correction and score only new tissue and subsequent inflorescence development against a matched control. | Escalate persistent abnormalities to pest microscopy, root-zone testing, tissue analysis, or a plant diagnostic laboratory rather than repeatedly reducing light without evidence.
prevention: Log canopy-level PPFD, photoperiod, air and leaf temperature, humidity or vapor-pressure deficit, carbon dioxide, and irrigation status by zone. | Map hot spots and irradiance gradients after fixture, HVAC, canopy-height, or density changes. | Retain cultivar- and stage-matched healthy reference sequences because published temperature optima and production responses vary among Cannabis genotypes.
warnings: Upward curl, tacoing, bleaching, pale tops, dry margins, and leaf angle are nonspecific and are not validated Cannabis heat- or light-stress ground truth without measured exposure and exclusion checks. | A controlled Stillwater trial produced linearly increasing inflorescence yield through 1,800 micromoles per square metre per second; therefore PPFD magnitude alone does not prove injury or define a universal damaging threshold. | Temperature optima for photosynthesis differed among tested drug- and fiber-type varieties, so 25, 30, 35, or 40 degrees Celsius must not be generalized into one cultivar-independent diagnosis. | The abnormal inflorescence-cluster observation came from defined 31/27 degrees Celsius flowering treatments in two genotypes and should be labeled treatment-associated, not universally heat-specific. | No reusable Cannabis symptom photograph with exposure measurements and adequate causal confirmation was admitted in this record; media remain empty rather than promoting anecdotal or vendor imagery.

name: Herbicide injury — clomazone-type bleaching
summary: A documented hemp chemical-injury differential in which soil-residual clomazone caused severe bleaching of newly formed tissue. The image pattern is not enough to identify the active ingredient; exposure history is essential.
affectedParts: newly formed leaves | shoot tips | whole plant depending on exposure
indicators: Newly formed tissue becomes markedly bleached after a plausible herbicide carryover or drift event | Multiple plants share an exposure-pattern distribution in the field or production area | Symptoms begin after a documented chemical application, carryover, contaminated medium, or drift event
exclusions: No plausible chemical exposure exists | Iron or sulfur deficiency is analytically supported and follows a root-zone pattern | Mites or systemic pathogens explain deformation and discoloration better | Bleaching maps tightly to high-light exposure rather than chemical distribution
lookAlikes: Iron deficiency | Sulfur deficiency | High-light bleaching | Broad mite injury | Genetic variegation
confirmation: Reconstruct spray, carryover, neighboring-field, substrate, and water-treatment history. | Use field pattern, timing, and where available laboratory residue analysis; do not identify clomazone from color alone.
immediateActions: Stop further suspected exposure and preserve records of all recent chemical applications. | Separate exposure investigation from nutrient correction so evidence is not erased.
correctivePlan: Address the confirmed exposure source and follow crop-specific professional guidance for affected plants and contaminated media/soil.
prevention: Maintain chemical-use records and review previous-crop residual restrictions before planting hemp. | Protect production areas from drift and contaminated equipment.
warnings: Bleached new growth is not clomazone-specific. | This profile does not recommend herbicide use; it is an injury-identification differential.

name: Alternaria leaf spot
summary: A laboratory-confirmed Cannabis leaf-spot disease. Brown lesions with yellow halos are compatible with Alternaria, but that appearance overlaps several hemp pathogens and must not be treated as species-level image ground truth.
affectedParts: leaves | leaf surface | whole canopy when severe
indicators: Small spots enlarge into brown irregular lesions with light yellow halos | Lesion centers may become fragile or perforated as disease advances | Multiple lesions can expand and merge on affected foliage
exclusions: Pycnidia strongly support a Septoria differential | Sooty underside conidial masses support Pseudocercospora | Round white-centered lesions with melanized conidiophores support Cercospora | No pathogen evidence is present and spray or contact injury maps to the lesion distribution
lookAlikes: Septoria leaf spot | Cercospora leaf spot | Bipolaris leaf spot | Anthracnose leaf spot | Bacterial leaf spot
confirmation: For species-level diagnosis use culture and/or validated molecular identification from representative lesions. | Photograph both surfaces and lesion distribution and preserve a sample before treatment.
immediateActions: Separate heavily affected propagation material and reduce avoidable leaf wetness while diagnosis is pending.
correctivePlan: Use a disease-management plan appropriate to the confirmed pathogen and production setting. | Remove heavily diseased debris when appropriate and monitor new lesions.
prevention: Avoid moving symptomatic plant material between clean areas. | Use sanitation and irrigation practices that limit prolonged leaf wetness.
warnings: Brown spots with yellow halos are not Alternaria-specific. | The primary report was one regional disease occurrence; prevalence varies by environment and production system.

name: Anthracnose leaf spot
summary: A confirmed Cannabis anthracnose leaf-spot disease. Tan-centered lesions can crack or drop out into shot-hole symptoms and coalesce into necrotic blotches, but those features still overlap other leaf-spot diseases.
affectedParts: leaves | lower canopy | leaf margins
indicators: Light-green specks become round or angular spots with tan centers, darker brown margins, and yellow halos | Lesion centers may crack or drop out, producing shot-hole or frog-eye appearance | Coalescing lesions can form larger necrotic regions and marginal lesions can cause scorching, puckering, or twisting
exclusions: Sooty underside conidial masses support Pseudocercospora | Pycnidia support Septoria | Laboratory testing identifies another leaf-spot pathogen | Physical holes occur without surrounding lesion development or pathogen evidence
lookAlikes: Cercospora leaf spot | Septoria leaf spot | Alternaria leaf spot | Bacterial leaf spot | Mechanical injury
confirmation: Use culture plus morphology and molecular identification when assigning Colletotrichum fioriniae. | Do not use shot-hole appearance alone as confirmation.
immediateActions: Preserve representative lesions for diagnosis and isolate heavily affected propagation material.
correctivePlan: Use pathogen-confirmed sanitation and disease management appropriate to the production system.
prevention: Reduce carryover of diseased debris and avoid prolonged foliage wetness where practical.
warnings: Shot-hole and frog-eye lesions are not species-specific. | The first report does not establish nationwide prevalence or a universal symptom sequence.

name: Bipolaris leaf spot
summary: A confirmed hemp leaf-spot and blight disease caused by Bipolaris gigantea. Necrosis can become severe, but lesion appearance overlaps Septoria, Cercospora, Alternaria, anthracnose, and abiotic damage.
affectedParts: leaves | canopy | buds secondarily when blight is severe
indicators: Necrotic leaf spots expand and can contribute to broader leaf blight | Disease can become widespread in outdoor hemp | Compatible lesions occur with Bipolaris conidia or molecular evidence from affected tissue
exclusions: Pycnidia dominate lesions | Cercospora-type conidiophores and white-centered round spots dominate | A chemical or physical injury pattern follows an exposure boundary | Laboratory testing identifies a different leaf-spot pathogen
lookAlikes: Septoria leaf spot | Cercospora leaf spot | Alternaria leaf spot | Anthracnose | Herbicide or contact injury
confirmation: Use fungal morphology and molecular identification from representative lesions for organism-level confirmation. | Record field distribution and lesion progression; one photograph is insufficient for B. gigantea.
immediateActions: Preserve symptomatic tissue for diagnosis before discarding representative samples. | Separate diseased material from clean propagation stock.
correctivePlan: Apply confirmed leaf-spot disease management appropriate to local rules and production conditions.
prevention: Reduce infected crop residue and prolonged leaf wetness where feasible. | Scout field plantings for early leaf spots.
warnings: Bipolaris leaf spot can look like several other Cannabis leaf-spot diseases. | Yield impact varies by cultivar, season, and disease complex.

name: Botrytis gray mold and bud rot
summary: A destructive Cannabis flower, stem, leaf, seedling, and postharvest disease associated with brown water-soaked or necrotic decay and, when conditions permit, gray to gray-brown sporulation. Internal flower decay can be poorly represented by an exterior view, and brown bud rot is not species-specific without laboratory confirmation.
affectedParts: developing and mature inflorescences | internal flower tissue | bracts and sugar leaves | stems and branch junctions | fan leaves under severe disease pressure | seedlings and cuttings | harvested and drying flower
stages: propagation | vegetative | flower | harvest and postharvest
indicators: One or more bracts or sugar leaves within a flower turn water-soaked, tan, or brown and collapse | Brown necrosis and mycelium occur inside a flower when it is carefully opened | Gray to gray-brown fuzzy growth or dusty spore masses develop on dead flower or stem tissue under humid conditions | Localized flower decay expands until much or all of an inflorescence is brown, dry-rotted, or collapsed | Stem lesions become pale or brown cankers and may split, girdle, or break; black sclerotia can occur | Under severe late-harvest pressure, small circular leaf spots can enlarge, merge, and become vein-delimited necrotic areas, sometimes with yellow margins | Multiple affected flowers cluster in dense, humid, poorly drying canopy zones and increase on serial inspection
exclusions: White superficial colonies occur without brown internal decay and microscopy supports powdery mildew | Only pistils or evenly aging leaves have browned while bracts, stems, and internal flower tissue remain firm and free of advancing lesions | Fusarium, Penicillium, or another mold is recovered from the active lesion instead of Botrytis | White cottony mycelium and the laboratory result support Sclerotinia rather than Botrytis | Damage stops after a documented heat, light, spray, or mechanical event and no mycelium, spores, or advancing rot develop | Caterpillars, frass, chewing, or webbing explain the localized flower collapse | A single postharvest discoloration image is available without intact-tissue context, environmental history, microscopy, culture, or molecular testing
lookAlikes: Fusarium flower mold or bud rot | Penicillium postharvest bud rot | Sclerotinia white mold | Powdery mildew | Normal pistil browning and late-flower senescence | Caterpillar or other boring-insect injury with frass | Heat, light, spray, or mechanical injury | Noninfectious postharvest browning
confirmation: Capture the affected flower exterior, a safely exposed interior cross-section, a close-up of the active lesion margin, surrounding flowers, and a whole-plant distribution view with scale; do not infer a clean interior from an exterior photograph. | Record serial change plus flowering or harvest stage, canopy location, temperature, relative humidity, condensation or wetness duration, irrigation or rain exposure, air movement, and drying conditions; these variables describe risk but do not confirm the organism. | With appropriate containment and protective procedures, sample the interface between advancing diseased and apparently healthy tissue rather than only dry dead tissue. | Submit representative flower or stem tissue to a plant diagnostic laboratory for microscopy and isolation plus a validated molecular or sequence-based assay when a Botrytis species label matters; request testing that considers Fusarium, Penicillium, Sclerotinia, and other flower molds. | Keep the image label at suspected gray mold or bud rot unless organism evidence is linked to the photographed plant and lesion; morphology or an environmental match alone is not laboratory confirmation.
immediateActions: Isolate or clearly mark suspect plants and stop moving affected flowers, tools, clothing, or debris through clean areas. | Avoid shaking or uncontained opening of visibly sporulating flowers; collect diagnostic images and samples with procedures that limit spore dispersal. | Separate visibly moldy harvested material from apparently clean material and do not consume or distribute it.
correctivePlan: Base crop removal, sanitation, environmental correction, and any treatment on the confirmed diagnosis, current local law, the production system, growth stage, and the current product label. | Reduce persistent tissue wetness and correct airflow or humidity problems documented in the affected zone without treating an environmental adjustment as proof that Botrytis caused the lesion. | Reinspect fixed flowers and neighboring plants over time; document new lesions and laboratory results, because old necrotic tissue will not recover.
prevention: Scout both exterior and protected interior flower zones during flowering and before harvest, especially where tissue dries slowly. | Sanitize tools between plants, remove crop debris without dispersing it, and prevent infected propagation or harvested material from entering clean zones. | Maintain traceable records linking plant, room or field position, media, environmental logs, sample identifier, and laboratory result.
warnings: Brown flower decay, gray fuzz, humidity, or a damaged sugar leaf alone is not species-level ground truth; multiple fungi and noninfectious injuries overlap visually. | Opening diseased flowers can expose hidden decay but can also release spores; use containment and appropriate protective procedures. | Temperature and humidity ranges reported by institutions are conducive-condition context, not universal diagnostic thresholds. | The CC BY composite figure is reference-only pending panel-level annotation and dataset-split review; the three university photographs have no explicit reuse license and remain hidden metadata references. | Do not use or distribute visibly mold-contaminated flower.

name: Cercospora leaf spot
summary: A Cannabis leaf-spot disease that often begins on older lower leaves as yellow flecks and develops into round lesions with pale centers, dark borders, and yellow halos. Conidiophore and laboratory evidence are needed because several pathogens make similar spots.
affectedParts: older lower-canopy leaves | leaf lesions | whole canopy as disease spreads
indicators: Small yellow flecks appear first on older lower foliage | Lesions become round, approximately 2 to 6 mm, with tan-to-white centers | Dark brown to purplish raised borders and yellow halos may develop | Melanized conidiophores can become visible in lesion centers
exclusions: Dark pycnidia support Septoria | Sooty underside masses support Pseudocercospora | Shot-hole lesions with Colletotrichum evidence support anthracnose | Laboratory testing identifies another pathogen
lookAlikes: Septoria leaf spot | Anthracnose | Alternaria leaf spot | Bipolaris leaf spot | Pseudocercospora olive leaf spot
confirmation: Inspect lesion centers with magnification and submit tissue for fungal identification. | Use morphology and/or molecular testing before assigning Cercospora cf. flagellaris at species level.
immediateActions: Document early lower-canopy distribution and preserve representative lesions.
correctivePlan: Use confirmed leaf-spot disease management and sanitation appropriate to the setting.
prevention: Scout older foliage and reduce avoidable leaf wetness. | Avoid moving symptomatic material into clean areas.
warnings: Round pale-centered lesions are not unique to Cercospora. | Cercospora often appears as part of a multi-pathogen field leaf-spot complex.

name: Exserohilum / Helminthosporium leaf blight
summary: A confirmed outdoor hemp leaf and stem spot disease. Round brown-to-black lesions with dark margins are compatible, but abundant conidia and laboratory identification are needed because the lesion appearance overlaps other leaf spots.
affectedParts: leaves | stems | canopy
indicators: Round brown-to-black lesions develop on leaves or stems | Lesions have distinctly darkened margins | Abundant large conidia can be observed within compatible lesions | ITS/RPB2 or equivalent fungal identification supports Exserohilum/Setosphaeria
exclusions: Pycnidia strongly support Septoria | Pale-centered lesions with Cercospora structures support Cercospora | Sooty underside masses support Pseudocercospora | No fungal evidence exists and chemical or mechanical injury follows an exposure pattern
lookAlikes: Bipolaris leaf spot | Septoria leaf spot | Cercospora leaf spot | Alternaria leaf spot | Bacterial leaf spot
confirmation: Examine lesion structures microscopically and use culture plus molecular identification for organism-level confirmation. | Photograph both surfaces and stem lesions before sampling.
immediateActions: Preserve representative lesions and reduce transfer of symptomatic debris into clean areas.
correctivePlan: Use confirmed leaf-blight management and sanitation appropriate to the production system.
prevention: Scout field foliage and stems and reduce prolonged leaf wetness where practical.
warnings: “Helminthosporium” is a historical/common disease name and does not by itself identify the modern fungal taxon. | Dark round spots are not Exserohilum-specific.

name: Fusarium foliar, flower and head blight complex
summary: A Cannabis Fusarium disease complex affecting leaves, flowers, drying floral material, stems and grain heads. It must be separated from Fusarium root/crown rot because infection site, symptom pattern and confirmation evidence differ.
affectedParts: leaves | flowers | grain heads | drying floral material | stems
indicators: Floral surfaces develop abundant hyphae with light-brown necrotic tips | Leaves develop roughly circular light-brown lesions with darker brown margins and gray-brown aging centers | Blight is centered on floral/head tissue rather than beginning as root decay | Fusarium macroconidia, culture, sequence or species-specific molecular evidence accompanies compatible tissue
exclusions: Root/crown rot and vascular wilt dominate without foliar or floral lesions | Gray fuzzy sporulation and diagnostic evidence identify Botrytis | White mold and sclerotia identify a Sclerotinia or southern-blight differential | No Fusarium evidence is present and drying/heat/mechanical injury explains floral browning
lookAlikes: Botrytis gray mold / bud rot | Sclerotinia white mold | Alternaria leaf spot | Bipolaris leaf spot | Fusarium crown/root rot
confirmation: Submit representative fresh lesion/flower tissue for culture and molecular identification when Fusarium species matters. | For suspected F. graminearum, species-specific molecular assays can detect infection that is not yet visually obvious.
immediateActions: Separate suspect floral material from clean material and preserve diagnostic samples before treatment or disposal. | Inspect roots/crowns separately so root Fusarium is not conflated with foliar/flower blight.
correctivePlan: Use laboratory-supported disease management and sanitation appropriate to the production stage and local crop rules.
prevention: Use clean propagation/seed sources where applicable and reduce movement of symptomatic plant debris. | Track humidity, rainfall/leaf wetness, and flower-stage disease development without treating environment as proof of pathogen identity.
warnings: Fusarium flower browning is not visually species-specific. | The 2020 survey identified both F. equiseti and F. graminearum in the foliar/flower blight complex; do not collapse every lesion into F. graminearum. | Image-only absence cannot exclude latent F. graminearum infection.

name: Powdery mildew
summary: A white superficial fungal growth that forms expanding powdery colonies on leaves, stems, petioles, and reproductive tissue.
affectedParts: leaf surface | stem | flower
indicators: White powder on leaves | Patches expand across surfaces | Powder can transfer when touched
exclusions: Residue follows droplet outlines after spraying | Webbing or insects are visible | The pale area is inside the tissue and cannot be disturbed
lookAlikes: Foliar spray residue | Mineral deposits | Trichomes on floral tissue
confirmation: Inspect colony margins with magnification. | Use a plant diagnostic lab when legal or commercial decisions depend on certainty.
immediateActions: Isolate affected material and reduce spore movement. | Stop overhead wetting and review humidity/airflow.
correctivePlan: Use legal stage-appropriate controls and sanitation. | Remove heavily affected tissue without dispersing spores.
prevention: Maintain clean intake material and stable humidity. | Inspect dense interior canopy zones.
warnings: Do not consume visibly mold-contaminated material. | Do not assume every white mark is mildew.

name: Pseudocercospora olive / sooty leaf spot
summary: A molecularly documented Cannabis leaf-spot disease characterized in one report by olive-to-pale lesions and sooty sporulation on the lower leaf surface. The underside view is important because upper-surface spots alone overlap many pathogens.
affectedParts: leaves | lower leaf surface | vein-limited tissue
indicators: Olive or pale yellowish leaf spots are present | Lesions can be vein-limited, irregular to subcircular, and several millimeters across | Lower leaf surfaces develop grey-brown to sooty conidial masses associated with lesions
exclusions: No underside sporulation is present and a different leaf-spot pathogen is confirmed | Pycnidia support Septoria | White-centered round lesions with Cercospora structures support Cercospora
lookAlikes: Septoria leaf spot | Cercospora leaf spot | Alternaria leaf spot | Downy mildew | Powdery mildew residue
confirmation: Photograph both leaf surfaces and inspect underside growth with magnification. | Use fungal morphology plus multilocus molecular identification for species-level confirmation.
immediateActions: Preserve sporulating tissue for diagnosis and reduce movement of symptomatic leaves.
correctivePlan: Use confirmed fungal leaf-spot management appropriate to the production system.
prevention: Scout both leaf surfaces and reduce prolonged foliage wetness.
warnings: Olive spots alone are not diagnostic. | The strongest modern Cannabis evidence is regional and species identification depends on morpho-molecular methods.

name: Sclerotinia white mold / crown rot complex
summary: A confirmed Cannabis Sclerotinia disease complex that can involve white-mold, crown-rot, wilt, and yellowing syndromes. S. sclerotiorum and S. minor are both documented on Cannabis/hemp; organism-level evidence is required because Botrytis, Fusarium, southern blight, and other molds overlap visually.
affectedParts: stems | crown | leaves | whole plant | flowering tissue depending on infection site
indicators: White fungal growth occurs on symptomatic Cannabis tissue with associated wilt or yellowing | Affected tissue declines in a pattern consistent with an active stem/crown or aerial infection | Laboratory isolation or DNA evidence identifies Sclerotinia sclerotiorum
exclusions: Gray mold and laboratory evidence identify Botrytis | Root/crown testing identifies Fusarium or Pythium instead | White residue is nonliving spray/mineral material | No organism evidence accompanies nonspecific wilt
lookAlikes: Botrytis gray mold | Fusarium wilt / crown rot | Pythium root rot | Powdery mildew | Nonliving spray residue
confirmation: Use culture and molecular identification for Sclerotinia confirmation. | Photograph infection site, internal stem/crown condition when available, and whole-plant distribution.
immediateActions: Isolate strongly affected plants and preserve diagnostic tissue before disposal.
correctivePlan: Use laboratory-confirmed disease management and sanitation appropriate to the setting.
prevention: Limit carryover of infected plant debris and conditions that keep susceptible tissue wet for extended periods.
warnings: White mold appearance is not specific to Sclerotinia. | The 2025 Cannabis pathogenicity report supports the organism as a real disease cause but not image-only species identification. | Sclerotinia sclerotiorum and S. minor should not be separated by canopy appearance alone; crown signs, sclerotia, culture, and molecular evidence carry more weight.

name: Septoria leaf spot complex
summary: A lower- and inner-canopy hemp leaf-spot syndrome caused by Septoria species. Dark pycnidia within expanding brown-gray lesions are useful evidence, but modern work shows more than one Septoria species can infect Cannabis.
affectedParts: older lower leaves | inner canopy leaves | leaf lesions
indicators: Disease often begins on lower or inner-canopy leaves | Small irregular brown-to-gray spots expand to several millimeters | Dark round pycnidia can be visible within lesions | Older leaves may defoliate as disease advances
exclusions: Sooty conidial masses on the underside support Pseudocercospora | White-centered round lesions with a pronounced dark border support Cercospora as a differential | Shot-hole lesions and Colletotrichum evidence support anthracnose | No fungal structures or lab evidence are present and an abiotic exposure fits the distribution better
lookAlikes: Cercospora leaf spot | Bipolaris leaf spot | Alternaria leaf spot | Pseudocercospora olive leaf spot | Anthracnose
confirmation: Examine lesions for pycnidia and submit representative tissue for fungal identification when species matters. | Use morphology and molecular sequence data for species-level Septoria classification because S. cannabis and S. cannabicola cannot be separated by a generic spot photo.
immediateActions: Document lower-versus-upper canopy distribution and both leaf surfaces. | Limit movement of symptomatic foliage into clean production areas.
correctivePlan: Use confirmed-disease sanitation and environmental management appropriate to the system. | Track new lesion development after intervention.
prevention: Scout lower and inner canopy foliage early. | Reduce prolonged leaf wetness and carryover of infected debris where practical.
warnings: Septoria species taxonomy on Cannabis is not reducible to visual symptoms. | Do not train a species classifier from mixed Septoria figures without organism-confirmed labels.

name: Southern blight
summary: A warm-condition soilborne Cannabis disease centered at the soil line, crown and taproot. White cottony mycelium plus tan-to-brown spherical sclerotia at the plant base are strong signs, but wilt alone is nonspecific.
affectedParts: lower stem at soil line | crown | taproot | root surface | whole plant
indicators: Dark brown-to-tan discoloration develops near the soil line | Rot extends into crown or taproot while foliage yellows and the plant wilts/collapses | White cottony mycelium develops on basal tissue or adjacent soil | Numerous spherical tan-to-dark-brown sclerotia occur with compatible basal rot
exclusions: No basal rot, mycelium or sclerotia are present and measured drought explains wilt | Laboratory evidence identifies Rhizoctonia, Fusarium, Pythium or another root/crown pathogen | White growth is confined to leaves/flowers without basal disease
lookAlikes: Rhizoctonia root rot / sore shin | Fusarium crown/root rot | Pythium root rot | Sclerotinia white mold | Severe root-zone hypoxia
confirmation: Inspect the soil line/crown/root surface for characteristic mycelium and sclerotia and submit tissue/culture for organism confirmation. | Record temperature/moisture context, but do not use hot wet conditions as diagnostic proof.
immediateActions: Isolate affected root-zone material and prevent movement of contaminated soil or debris to clean areas. | Preserve basal tissue and sclerotia for diagnostic testing.
correctivePlan: Use confirmed soilborne-disease sanitation and crop-legal management appropriate to the setting. | Address excess moisture where measured without assuming moisture correction eliminates established pathogen inoculum.
prevention: Avoid moving contaminated soil or plant debris between production areas. | Monitor crown/root health during warm wet periods.
warnings: Whole-plant wilt alone cannot identify southern blight. | Sclerotia and laboratory evidence are substantially stronger than canopy appearance.

name: Stable chlorotic sectoring / suspected genetic variegation
summary: Sharply bounded chlorotic or chlorophyll-deficient sectors can be consistent with somatic mutation or mosaicism in Cannabis, but no published Cannabis image morphology proves genetic cause; treat this as an exclusion-based phenotype until serial lineage evidence and appropriate laboratory work support the attribution.
affectedParts: individual leaflet sectors | entire leaflet portions | successive leaves from one shoot or meristem | one branch or clonal lineage | whole plant only when a documented cultivar trait is established
stages: vegetative | flowering; stage specificity is not established
indicators: Abrupt yellow, cream, pale-green, or near-white tissue adjoining normally green tissue within the same leaf | Sector-shaped or longitudinal pigment loss rather than uniform whole-leaf yellowing | The same shoot position or clonal lineage is mapped across successive leaves and time rather than inferred from one detached leaf | Affected tissue retains its boundary while new observations document whether the pattern remains localized, expands, disappears, or is joined by distortion and stunting | Matched images preserve upper and lower leaf surfaces, whole-plant distribution, branch identity, scale, cultivar, developmental stage, and camera-lighting conditions
exclusions: Validated testing detects a virus or viroid consistent with the sampled tissue and syndrome | Mosaic, mottling, line patterns, curling, brittle growth, shortened internodes, stunting, or reduced inflorescence performance progress beyond the original sector | Chlorosis follows leaf age, interveinal or marginal patterns, or a measured tissue-nutrient, substrate-pH, or root-zone-EC abnormality better than a branch lineage | Microscopy or organism sampling confirms thrips, mites, leafminers, or another pest associated with the marks | The distribution maps to a lamp, spray, pesticide, plant-growth regulator, abrasion, heat event, or other documented exposure | Camera white balance, glare, shadow, senescence, or cultivar pigmentation explains the apparent color boundary
lookAlikes: Mosaic, mottling, or line-pattern syndrome of unresolved cause | Beet curly top virus disease | Hop latent viroid | Lettuce chlorosis virus or other regional virus | Iron, manganese, magnesium, or nitrogen disorder | Root-zone pH or EC disorder | Thrips, mites, or leafminer injury | Herbicide or plant-growth-regulator injury | Spray or high-light injury | Normal senescence or cultivar pigmentation | Camera color, glare, or shadow artifact
confirmation: Do not confirm genetic variegation, chimerism, mutation, virus freedom, or training ground truth from a photograph or video. | Record the exact leaf, node, branch, plant, cultivar, propagation source, date, stage, lighting, and serial change; include healthy plants of the same cultivar and environment. | Inspect both leaf surfaces and protected growth with magnification, and document pest organisms or their absence separately from the color phenotype. | Measure root-zone pH and EC and review irrigation, tissue or solution analysis, nutrient history, spray records, lamp position, temperature, and mechanical injury before assigning a developmental explanation. | Submit symptomatic and matched asymptomatic tissue to a plant diagnostic laboratory for a locally appropriate validated virus/viroid differential; a negative targeted assay excludes only the agents and sample covered by that assay. | When a genetic attribution is operationally important, compare mapped sectors and clones and use qualified genetic or meristem-lineage analysis; persistence alone is supportive context, not proof.
immediateActions: Keep the visual label at “chlorotic sectoring—cause unresolved” and flag it for human review. | Pause distribution of suspect cuttings and separate them from verified genetic-trait references until infectious causes are reasonably excluded. | Preserve serial imagery and matched tissue before pruning or discarding the affected shoot.
correctivePlan: Correct only measured root-zone, nutrient, pest, or exposure problems and document whether new growth changes. | If validated pathogen testing is positive, move the sample to the confirmed pathogen class and follow the facility’s sanitation and plant-health protocol. | If differential testing is negative and the pattern tracks a shoot or clone, retain a “suspected genetic/developmental” label unless genetic evidence supports a stronger claim.
prevention: Maintain cultivar, mother-plant, cutting-position, and clone-lineage records. | Use tested propagation stock and tool-sanitation practices so a stable-looking pattern is not assumed noninfectious. | Capture healthy reference plants under repeatable lighting and camera settings for color comparison.
warnings: “Genetic mosaicism” describes within-organism genetic variation; a visible “mosaic symptom” is not evidence of that mechanism. | The Cannabis mosaicism sequencing study sampled one mother plant and did not link its variants to visible leaf sectors. | The VIGS bleaching experiment was an intentionally virus-vector-induced gene-silencing phenotype and must not be treated as proof that natural bleaching is inherited or noninfectious. | The composite reference image mixes four unresolved mosaic-like presentations with panel e, which the authors characterize as somatic-mutation-associated chlorotic sectors; preserve panel labels and never train the entire composite as one genetic class. | Negative molecular, microscopy, or indicator-host findings are bounded by sample quality, agent coverage, assay performance, and observation time. | This reviewed record validates an uncertainty-bounded workflow, not image-only genetic ground truth; all symptom-only samples remain human-review items.

name: Armyworm caterpillar feeding complex
summary: A late-season caterpillar feeding differential for hemp. Armyworm larvae can defoliate foliage and enter buds or flowers, but species-level identification requires larval morphology rather than damage pattern alone.
affectedParts: leaves | leaf midribs | buds | flowers
indicators: Caterpillar larvae are present with fresh irregular chewing injury | Severe feeding skeletonizes or strips leaves toward the midribs | Larvae entering buds or flowers leave feeding injury together with silk and frass | Larval head/body markings support fall armyworm, true armyworm, or another armyworm identification
exclusions: No larvae or fresh frass are found and damage is old | Characteristic looping larvae support cabbage looper | Adult Japanese beetles are actively skeletonizing tissue
lookAlikes: Cabbage looper | Corn-earworm-like caterpillar injury | Japanese beetle | Other noctuid larvae
confirmation: Collect or clearly photograph representative larvae and use morphology for species-level assignment. | Treat frass plus an active larva as stronger evidence than holes alone.
immediateActions: Inspect fresh feeding fronts, buds, and flowers for larvae and frass. | Record larval size and density because damage potential changes with instar and population.
correctivePlan: Use an IPM response based on confirmed caterpillar identity, population, crop stage, and locally legal hemp options.
prevention: Scout late-season foliage and reproductive tissue for egg masses and young larvae. | Use monitoring and beneficial-conservation practices where appropriate.
warnings: Armyworm damage overlaps other caterpillar feeding. | Do not identify species from leaf holes or frass alone.

name: Cabbage looper feeding injury
summary: A caterpillar chewing pest documented on hemp foliage and floral buds. Irregular holes are low-specificity; the looping green larva and fresh feeding site make the diagnosis substantially stronger.
affectedParts: leaf undersides | lower leaves | upper foliage as feeding progresses | floral buds
indicators: Green caterpillars with pale side striping move in a characteristic looping gait on hemp | Large irregular chewing holes begin on leaf tissue, often from lower-leaf undersides | Severe feeding strips foliage or damages/deforms floral buds
exclusions: No larvae, frass, or active chewing are found | Larval morphology supports armyworm or another caterpillar | Skeletonization occurs with aggregating adult Japanese beetles
lookAlikes: Armyworm feeding | Japanese beetle | Spotted cucumber beetle | Other caterpillars
confirmation: Find and document the larva on or near fresh damage and use morphology/behavior for identification. | Use chewing pattern only as supporting evidence.
immediateActions: Inspect undersides and flowers for larvae, eggs, frass, and fresh chewing. | Record larval density rather than treating one old hole as an active infestation.
correctivePlan: Use threshold-aware IPM and locally legal hemp controls for confirmed active feeding.
prevention: Scout lower foliage and reproductive tissue during late-season moth activity. | Conserve beneficial predators and parasitoids where compatible with the IPM program.
warnings: Irregular holes are shared by many chewing insects. | Old feeding damage can remain after the pest is gone.

name: Dectes stem-borer injury
summary: A stem-boring beetle differential for hemp. Internal pith galleries plus a compatible larva or adult are much stronger evidence than wilting or stem breakage alone.
affectedParts: main stems | pith | stem nodes | whole shoot secondarily
indicators: Internal stem or pith galleries are present | Cream-colored longhorn-beetle larvae occur inside affected stems or compatible gray long-antenna adults are found nearby | Infested stems may swell, split, wilt, die back, or break where internal tunneling weakens them
exclusions: Stem interior lacks galleries and a vascular/root pathogen explains wilt | Boring is produced by another identified stem-boring insect | Breakage is purely mechanical with healthy intact pith
lookAlikes: Fusarium stem/crown disease | Mechanical stem splitting | Other stem borers | Drought-related wilt
confirmation: Split a representative symptomatic stem lengthwise and document galleries and larvae. | Identify the insect when species-level attribution matters.
immediateActions: Flag and inspect affected stems before disposal so internal evidence is preserved. | Scout adjacent plants for adults, entry sites, or galleries.
correctivePlan: Use an IPM plan appropriate to confirmed stem-borer pressure and locally legal hemp practices.
prevention: Scout stems for swelling, entry injury, and adults during the relevant field season. | Remove or manage infested residues when locally appropriate.
warnings: Wilt and stem breakage are nonspecific. | A gallery without an identified insect should remain a generic stem-borer diagnosis.

name: Japanese beetle feeding injury
summary: A conspicuous adult beetle pest of hemp. Skeletonized leaves are compatible with feeding, but the metallic green-and-bronze adult and aggregated active feeding provide the strongest field evidence.
affectedParts: leaves | flowers | tender shoots
indicators: Metallic green adults with bronze wing covers are actively feeding on hemp | Leaf tissue between veins is consumed, leaving a lace-like or skeletonized appearance | Beetles may aggregate on exposed foliage or reproductive tissue
exclusions: No beetles are present and another defoliator is actively feeding | Damage is mined within leaf tissue rather than skeletonized from the surface | Skeletonization is old and no current infestation can be established
lookAlikes: Other scarab beetles | Caterpillar defoliation | Spotted cucumber beetle
confirmation: Photograph adults with fresh damage and verify the characteristic adult morphology. | Do not assign Japanese beetle from skeletonization alone.
immediateActions: Count active beetles and estimate fresh defoliation rather than using cumulative old injury. | Scout nearby sun-exposed foliage and flowers.
correctivePlan: Use IPM appropriate to verified beetle pressure and locally legal hemp options.
prevention: Scout during seasonal adult emergence and record aggregation patterns. | Avoid assuming pheromone traps reduce damage; trapping can alter local beetle aggregation.
warnings: Skeletonization is not unique to Japanese beetle. | Economic thresholds established for other crops should not be copied directly to hemp without hemp-specific validation.

name: Spotted cucumber beetle feeding injury
summary: A documented industrial-hemp chewing pest. Adult beetles can damage foliage and floral tissue while larvae can injure root hairs and root tips; organism evidence is needed because ragged holes and weak roots are not species-specific.
affectedParts: leaves | leaf margins | flowers | pollen-bearing tissue | root hairs | root tips
indicators: Yellow-green adult beetles with twelve dark spots are present on hemp | Leaves or floral tissue show fresh holes and ragged chewing edges while adults are feeding | Root injury or weak anchorage occurs together with compatible rootworm larvae in the root zone
exclusions: No compatible beetles or larvae are found and another chewing pest is present | Damage consists mainly of stippling, silvering, mining, or sap-feeding distortion rather than chewing | Root decline occurs without root-feeding larvae and a pathogen or irrigation disorder is better supported
lookAlikes: Japanese beetle | Armyworm / caterpillar feeding | Cabbage looper | Mechanical tearing | Root disease
confirmation: Photograph or collect the beetle/larva with the damaged tissue; identify the organism rather than assigning species from holes alone. | Inspect roots only when root symptoms or lodging are present.
immediateActions: Scout nearby plants for adults and fresh feeding damage. | Document root-zone larvae separately from above-ground beetles.
correctivePlan: Use an IPM response appropriate to confirmed pest pressure, crop stage, and locally legal hemp options.
prevention: Scout field margins and foliage during vegetative to early flowering growth. | Reduce weed or alternate-host reservoirs where agronomically appropriate.
warnings: Chewing holes are not diagnostic of spotted cucumber beetle. | Root damage can coexist with root pathogens; finding beetle larvae does not exclude disease.

name: Tarnished plant bug feeding injury
summary: A piercing-sucking hemp pest that can injure expanding leaves, shoots, buds, and flowers. Terminal distortion and chlorotic spotting overlap mites and abiotic injury, so a compatible Lygus insect should be observed before assigning this diagnosis.
affectedParts: young leaves | shoot tips | stems | buds | flowers
indicators: Fast-moving mottled brown bugs with a pale or yellow triangular marking are present on symptomatic hemp | Young tissue develops chlorotic feeding spots, curling, or distorted terminal growth | Developing buds are malformed or abort while compatible plant bugs are feeding
exclusions: No compatible insects are found after repeated scouting | Microscopy confirms broad or russet mites | Distortion follows a chemical, heat, or mechanical exposure pattern | Chewing holes dominate rather than piercing-sucking injury
lookAlikes: Broad mite | Hemp russet mite | Boron deficiency | Herbicide injury | Stink bug feeding
confirmation: Capture or clearly photograph the insect on symptomatic tissue and use morphology for species-level identification. | Treat terminal distortion alone as low-specificity evidence.
immediateActions: Scout young leaves, terminals, and buds for nymphs/adults. | Record whether injury is clustered along field edges or alternate-host vegetation.
correctivePlan: Use confirmed-pest IPM and locally legal hemp controls only when population and injury justify intervention.
prevention: Monitor weeds and field margins that can harbor plant bugs. | Scout during rapid terminal and bud development.
warnings: Curling and distorted buds are not Lygus-specific. | Do not infer this pest from one deformed leaf without organism evidence.

name: Thrips feeding injury
summary: Onion thrips and western flower thrips are documented on hemp; feeding can produce vein-associated white flecks or irregular silvery scars, dark fecal spots, and distortion of leaves damaged while expanding, but symptoms alone cannot identify the insect or its species.
affectedParts: leaf upper and lower surfaces | leaf veins and adjacent lamina | young expanding leaves | growing tips | flowers and pollen-bearing tissue
indicators: Irregular white flecks or silvery scarred patches, often following or crossing veins | Small dark fecal spots occur within or beside fresh feeding scars | Minute elongated yellow, tan, or yellow-brown insects are recovered from symptomatic tissue | Wingless creamy-yellow larvae or slender adults with narrow fringed wings are visible under magnification | Leaves fed on while developing later expand with localized distortion or uneven scarred areas | Indoor or protected-crop injury increases over serial observations while matched uninfested plants remain unchanged
exclusions: No thrips, larvae, shed skins, or dark fecal spots are found after repeat inspection, foliage tapping, and sticky-card monitoring | Fine webbing, round eggs, and two-spotted mites are present | Microscopic cigar-shaped mites with two pairs of legs are present | Only residue is visible and it wipes or dissolves without damaged epidermal tissue beneath it | The pattern follows a nutrient-mobility gradient by leaf age rather than localized feeding scars | Circular or angular lesions enlarge independently and have halos, fungal growth, bacterial streaming, or pathogen-positive laboratory results | Distortion is restricted to the newest protected tissue and broad mites or dotted broad-mite eggs are confirmed | Abrasion aligns uniformly with a fan, rubbing surface, spray event, or physical contact and no organisms are recovered
lookAlikes: Two-spotted spider mites | Hemp russet mite | Broad mite | Foliar spray or mineral residue | Wind or contact abrasion | Edema or physiological corking | Nutrient or root-zone disorder | Leaf-spot pathogen | Beneficial predatory thrips
confirmation: Inspect both leaf surfaces, veins, folds, growing tips, and flowers with at least a 10× hand lens; record whether scars, dark fecal spots, larvae, adults, and shed skins occur together. | Tap symptomatic foliage and flowers over white paper or a collection tray, then preserve representative insects for magnified examination. | Use blue or yellow sticky cards as population and movement monitors, not as proof that a particular damaged leaf was caused by thrips. | For species-level labels, submit intact adults to an entomology or plant diagnostic laboratory for morphological or validated molecular identification; color and a routine phone photograph are insufficient. | Capture serial whole-plant, leaf-surface macro, opposite-surface, vein-level, and organism-magnification views with scale and production context; compare with a matched healthy plant.
immediateActions: Separate or clearly mark suspect plants and inspect neighboring propagation material, young growth, flowers, weeds, and sticky cards before moving plants. | Preserve representative insects and pre-treatment images before intervention when species or causal confirmation is needed. | Avoid applying an unverified pesticide or coating simply because silver injury is present.
correctivePlan: Use only a control program legal for Cannabis or hemp, the jurisdiction, production system, and growth stage, following the current product label and worker-safety requirements. | Track fresh scars and organism counts at fixed sampling sites; old silver scars and distorted leaves will not heal and should not be used alone to judge control. | Address confirmed entry or reservoir points such as infested transplants, weeds, crop debris, flowers, or unscreened openings while conserving identified beneficial thrips and other natural enemies.
prevention: Quarantine and hand-lens inspect incoming clones and transplants. | Scout representative plants and canopy zones on a fixed schedule, including young leaves and flowers rather than relying only on sticky cards. | Maintain clean plant and weed-free buffer practices appropriate to the production system and record thrips detections by stage and location.
warnings: Silver flecks, black specks, or distorted leaves alone are not thrips ground truth; confirm the organism and feeding context. | A group-level thrips label does not establish onion thrips, western flower thrips, tobacco thrips, or another species; species identification requires suitable adult specimens and specialist examination. | The controlled yield study was preliminary and used defined indoor infestation treatments; it does not establish a universal economic threshold or symptom-to-yield conversion. | Predatory thrips can be beneficial, so the presence of a thrips-shaped insect is not sufficient to assign a damaging-pest label. | The two institutional Cannabis images below have no explicit reuse license; they are hidden metadata references, not copied assets or training samples.

name: Broad mite
summary: A microscopic tarsonemid mite that hides in protected young tissue; feeding injury appears later as hardened, puckered, cupped, or strap-like new leaves, bronzing, short internodes, and deformed buds.
affectedParts: youngest expanding leaves | leaf undersides | leaf axils | growing tips | flower buds | shaded or protected canopy tissue
indicators: Warped, puckered, or hardened newest leaves | Cupped or strap-like new growth | Bronze, copper, or dark discoloration on young tissue | Short internodes and stunted growing tips | Deformed or aborted flower buds | Oval mites or dotted translucent eggs under magnification
exclusions: Cigar-shaped mites with only two pairs of legs are present instead | Fine webbing and round spider-mite eggs are present | Only older leaves follow a mobile-nutrient symptom pattern | Injury is uniform on the brightest upper canopy and measured leaf temperature or light is excessive | No mites or dotted eggs are found after repeat sampling of adjacent fresh growth and protected sites
lookAlikes: Hemp russet mite | Cyclamen mite | Heat or light stress | Plant-growth-regulator herbicide injury | Micronutrient or root-zone disorder | Virus-like or developmental distortion
confirmation: Inspect fresh expanding tissue adjacent to the worst damage, including undersides, axils, growing tips, and buds, at about 20× or with a dissecting microscope. | Confirm translucent oval adults and clear oval eggs bearing raised pale dots; adult females may show a pale dorsal stripe. | Separate broad mite from cigar-shaped, two-pair-legged russet mites and from cyclamen mites, whose eggs lack the characteristic dotted surface. | Treat a negative sample cautiously because injury can persist after mites leave badly damaged tissue; repeat sampling across plants and time when suspicion remains.
immediateActions: Quarantine suspect plants and stop moving cuttings or shared tools into clean areas. | Microscope-screen neighboring plants before choosing any control.
correctivePlan: Use only controls legal for the crop, jurisdiction, and growth stage, following the current label. | Track mites or eggs on fixed fresh-growth sampling sites; do not judge response from old distorted leaves. | Remove severely infested material without spreading mites and sanitize shared tools between plants.
prevention: Start with inspected propagation material. | Quarantine and magnification-screen incoming clones. | Include protected new-growth sites in routine scouting rather than inspecting only mature fan leaves.
warnings: Leaf distortion, bronzing, or short internodes alone are not diagnostic. | The two media assets below show the organism without a host and are morphology references, not cannabis symptom ground truth. | Although their licenses permit reuse, both remain reference-only and excluded from automated training pending a separate training and dataset-split review.

name: Hemp russet mite
summary: A microscopic eriophyid mite whose feeding can cause localized bronzing, brittle or reduced leaves, distorted edges, stunting, and suppressed floral growth without the webbing typical of spider mites.
affectedParts: young leaves | leaf undersides | petioles | stems | growing tips | flower buds
indicators: Dull gray or bronzed foliage | Brittle or reduced leaf size | Leaf edges curl upward or downward | Stem or petiole bronzing | Stunted growing tips | No webbing despite mite-like damage
exclusions: Fine webbing and round spider-mite eggs are present | Only interveinal chlorosis follows an older-leaf nutrient pattern | Damage is restricted to the hottest or brightest canopy surface | No cigar-shaped mites are found after adequate microscope sampling
lookAlikes: Two-spotted spider mites | Thrips | Broad mites | Heat or light stress | Nutrient or root-zone stress | Powdery residue
confirmation: Sample both symptomatic and adjacent apparently healthy leaves; inspect undersides, midribs, petioles, and protected trichome zones with a dissecting or digital microscope. | Confirm pale, cigar-shaped eriophyid mites with only two pairs of legs; ordinary phone or whole-plant images are not sufficient. | For repeatable image counts, photograph multiple leaflet sections under microscope magnification rather than relying on a single field of view.
immediateActions: Quarantine suspect plants and stop moving cuttings, tools, clothing, or plant debris into clean areas. | Inspect nearby plants under adequate magnification before choosing a treatment.
correctivePlan: Use only controls legal for the crop, jurisdiction, and growth stage, following the current product label. | Track mite counts on fixed leaf positions after intervention; visible injury can lag behind population change. | Remove severely infested material without spreading mites and clean shared tools between plants.
prevention: Start with inspected, mite-free propagation material. | Quarantine and microscope-screen incoming clones. | Maintain routine microscope scouting because low populations can be visually silent.
warnings: Leaf curl or bronzing alone is not diagnostic. | Do not confuse tan cast-skin accumulations with fungal powder. | CC BY 4.0 permits reuse with attribution, but these hashed reference images remain excluded from model training until a separate training and dataset-split review is completed.

name: Two-spotted spider mites
summary: Sap-feeding mites cause fine stippling from the leaf underside and visible webbing as populations increase.
affectedParts: leaf underside | canopy | flower
indicators: Tiny yellow or white stipples | Fine webbing | Visible mites or eggs under magnification
exclusions: Silver scraped streaks with black specks | No organisms after careful underside inspection | Damage follows a nutrient-mobility pattern
lookAlikes: Thrips | Hemp russet mites | Spray residue
confirmation: Inspect undersides with 30–60× magnification. | Look for round eggs and moving mites.
immediateActions: Isolate affected plants. | Inspect nearby plants and remove heavily infested material safely.
correctivePlan: Use a legal crop- and stage-appropriate IPM rotation. | Repeat monitoring between treatments.
prevention: Quarantine incoming plants. | Scout leaf undersides weekly.
warnings: Avoid spraying unsuitable products on flowers. | Webbing indicates an established population, not an early case.

name: Root-knot nematodes
summary: A confirmed Cannabis root-parasitic nematode problem. Root galling with females/egg masses is far more discriminating than above-ground stunting or chlorosis, which overlap nearly every root-zone disorder.
affectedParts: roots | root galls | whole plant secondarily
indicators: Roots develop characteristic localized galls or knots | Females can be present inside galled root tissue with egg masses associated with roots | Plants may be stunted or chlorotic secondarily | Nematode morphology or molecular testing identifies Meloidogyne
exclusions: Root enlargements are normal lateral-root structures rather than galls | No galls/nematodes are found and a different root disease or abiotic condition is confirmed | Only canopy stunting/chlorosis is available without root inspection
lookAlikes: Rhizoctonia root rot | Fusarium root/crown disease | Root binding | Nutrient deficiency | Drought / water-deficit stress
confirmation: Wash and inspect the complete root system for true galls and collect roots/soil for nematode analysis. | Use adult/juvenile morphology and/or validated molecular assays when Meloidogyne species matters.
immediateActions: Prevent movement of potentially infested soil/root debris into clean production areas. | Preserve representative galled roots and surrounding soil for diagnosis.
correctivePlan: Base management on confirmed nematode identification, production system, and locally legal options.
prevention: Use clean planting material/media and avoid moving infested soil on tools/equipment. | Inspect roots when unexplained stunting occurs in field/container production.
warnings: Above-ground chlorosis and stunting are nonspecific and should have very low diagnostic weight without root evidence. | Cannabis yield-loss thresholds for root-knot nematodes remain incompletely defined.

name: Late-cycle leaf aging / senescence context
summary: Cannabis and hemp leaves can lose chlorophyll and photosynthetic capacity as foliage ages and flowering advances, with stronger age and canopy-position effects in older or lower leaves; visible yellowing is neither required nor sufficient to classify the change as normal senescence.
affectedParts: physiologically older fan leaves | lower-canopy fan leaves | upper-canopy fan leaves assessed separately | whole canopy only as a mapped age gradient | inflorescences and sugar leaves as exclusion-check tissue
stages: flowering time series; strongest Cannabis evidence compares weeks 1, 5, and 9 after transition to a 12-hour photoperiod
indicators: Change is gradual across serial observations rather than abrupt between captures | Older or lower-position fan leaves change before recently expanded upper-canopy leaves | Chlorophyll index or photosynthetic capacity declines with documented leaf age even when a leaf remains visibly green | The same cultivar and production cohort shows a repeatable late-cycle age and canopy-position gradient | Inflorescences, recently expanded leaves, stems, and roots lack independent evidence of a spreading disorder | Color assessment is made under calibrated or repeatable lighting with healthy same-cultivar references
exclusions: Visible yellowing alone is used as proof of senescence or harvest readiness | Recently expanded or upper-canopy leaves decline first or as strongly as older lower leaves without an established age gradient | Chlorosis begins early, progresses rapidly, reduces whole-plant vigor, or spreads independently of leaf age | Interveinal chlorosis, marginal scorch, discrete lesions, rings, mosaic, distortion, brittle growth, webbing, feeding scars, frass, or visible organisms are present | Root-zone pH, EC, water content, oxygenation, root appearance, or irrigation history is abnormal | Feed composition, tissue or solution analysis, or response to correction supports nitrogen or another nutrient disorder | Inflorescence mold, necrosis, odor, collapse, or laboratory evidence supports a pathogen | A lamp, spray, heat, cold, drought, salinity, or other exposure gradient explains the distribution better
lookAlikes: Nitrogen deficiency or under-supply during flowering | Magnesium, potassium, phosphorus, sulfur, or micronutrient disorder | Root-zone pH or EC disorder | Water shortage or excessive vapor demand | Overwatering or root hypoxia | Pythium, Phytophthora, Fusarium, or other root disease | Hop latent viroid | Beet curly top virus or unresolved systemic mosaic syndrome | Powdery mildew, Botrytis, or leaf-spot disease | Hemp russet mite, broad mite, spider mite, or thrips injury | High-light, heat, cold, spray, or plant-growth-regulator injury | Cultivar pigmentation or camera color artifact
confirmation: Do not label “normal fade,” senescence, ripeness, harvest readiness, nutrient depletion, or plant health from color in one photograph or video. | Record leaf node, leaf age, upper versus lower canopy, cultivar, flowering day, photoperiod, PPFD, temperature, humidity or vapor-pressure deficit, irrigation, and serial rate of change. | Capture whole-plant, canopy, branch, upper-leaf-surface, lower-leaf-surface, root-zone, and inflorescence views under repeatable lighting with a color reference and scale. | Measure root-zone pH, EC, water content or container weight, and inspect roots; review feed composition and, when consequential, use calibrated solution or tissue analysis rather than assuming remobilization. | Inspect both leaf surfaces and protected growth with magnification for mites, thrips, webbing, eggs, cast skins, frass, and feeding scars. | Use a plant diagnostic laboratory when lesions, systemic distortion, vascular or root decline, inflorescence disease, or virus/viroid signs remain plausible. | Compare several healthy same-cultivar plants from the same propagation cohort; an age-position gradient that repeats across serial observations is contextual support, not causal proof.
immediateActions: Keep the sample labeled “late-cycle leaf aging—cause unresolved” until exclusion checks are complete. | Preserve serial images and measured root-zone, environment, and nutrition records before changing the program. | Isolate or pause propagation from plants with systemic, pest, pathogen, or viroid warning signs.
correctivePlan: Correct only measured nutrient, pH, EC, irrigation, environment, pest, or pathogen problems; do not force yellowing or apply nitrogen solely from camera color. | Reassess recently expanded leaves, roots, and inflorescences after any evidence-based correction while recognizing that old yellow or necrotic tissue will not become a clean health indicator. | Retain the normal-development label only when progression remains slow, age-positioned, cultivar-consistent, and unsupported by competing diagnoses.
prevention: Maintain same-cultivar flowering timelines with leaf-node and canopy-position annotations. | Keep calibrated pH and EC records, irrigation history, environmental logs, pest scouting, and laboratory results linked to image and video samples. | Create healthy reference captures under fixed lighting and camera settings rather than relying on internet photographs or a universal week-of-flower chart.
warnings: A hemp leaf-aging study found photosynthetic capacity could decline while leaves remained green, so visible yellowing is not required for senescence. | The Stillwater flowering study found temporal and canopy-position changes but did not resolve how much was caused by leaf age versus whole-plant ontogeny and did not validate a universal visible fade. | Flowering Cannabis still responds materially to nitrogen and phosphorus supply; withholding nutrients to manufacture a fade is not evidence of normal development. | Color is not a validated harvest-maturity marker and this record does not recommend harvest timing, flushing, or a universal feeding concentration. | The source experiments used limited cultivars and defined production systems; their weeks and nutrient concentrations must not be generalized as thresholds. | No authoritative Cannabis photograph or video with adequate longitudinal measurements and causal exclusion was admitted; media remain empty rather than treating vendor, forum, anecdotal, or generated imagery as ground truth. | All symptom-only samples remain low confidence and require human review.

name: Cannabis reproductive sex expression
summary: Expressed sex is classified from reproductive organs, not seedling shape: pistillate flowers bear protruding stigmas, staminate flowers form stalked anther-bearing clusters, and co-sexual plants express both flower types or anthers within a pistillate inflorescence.
affectedParts: leaf axils and nodes | terminal and lateral inflorescences | flower bracts | stigmas | anthers
indicators: No reliable image-only sex distinction during the seedling or vegetative stage | Pistillate flowers with bifurcate protruding white-to-yellowish stigmas | Pedicillate clusters of staminate flowers that open to expose five anthers | Bright-yellow anthers within bract tissue among stigmas on a co-sexual inflorescence | Stigmas curl and brown or redden while bracts and carpels swell with pistillate-flower maturation
exclusions: A seedling or vegetative plant is labeled male or female from height, leaf size, vigor, or internode length alone | Only stipules, new axillary shoots, or unopened undifferentiated buds are visible | A single node or canopy view is used to exclude co-sexual expression | Yellow anther-like material is present but focus, scale, and surrounding flower organs are not visible | A Y-linked marker result is used to claim that female versus monoecious floral expression has been distinguished
lookAlikes: Stipules at the node | New axillary shoots | Unopened flower or leaf primordia | Swollen pistillate bracts | Senescing or damaged stigmas | Yellow plant debris or insect material inside an inflorescence
confirmation: Record focused macro views of several upper and lower nodes plus terminal and lateral inflorescences, including scale and the surrounding bract, stigma, or pedicel context. | Confirm pistillate expression from protruding stigmas and staminate expression from opened anther-bearing flowers rather than overall plant habit. | Repeat inspection through flowering because a few anthers can be hidden within dense pistillate tissue and may appear after an earlier negative view. | When pre-flower genetic sex is operationally important, use a validated Y-linked assay; interpret a negative result as female-or-monoecious genotype rather than proof of exclusively pistillate future expression.
immediateActions: Keep the visual label indeterminate when reproductive organs are not yet visible. | If pollen release matters to the production objective, isolate a plant with confirmed anthers while identity and facility-specific disposition are reviewed.
correctivePlan: Treat sex expression as a monitored developmental classification, not a nutrient or pesticide diagnosis. | Use serial, multi-location inspection to document whether staminate organs are isolated, plant-wide, or embedded within pistillate inflorescences. | Apply only the facility’s lawful crop-management protocol after expressed flower type is confirmed.
