name: Boron deficiency
summary: A controlled Cannabis boron-withholding disorder centered on growing tips, expanding leaves, and root tips. Severe new-growth distortion is useful supporting evidence, but diagnosis should be tied to nutrition and root-zone measurements rather than leaf shape alone.
affectedParts: growing tips | new and expanding leaves | leaf margins | root tips | whole plant in advanced cases
indicators: Growing tips become stunted before older foliage shows a dominant pattern | New leaflets are distorted, smaller, and narrow near the leaflet base | Advanced new growth curls inward, downward, or at irregular angles and develops marginal necrosis | Severe deficiency can kill growing tips and root tips and lead to whole-plant wilting
exclusions: Distorted tips contain broad mites or hemp russet mites | Root-zone boron supply and tissue analysis are adequate while another exposure explains the distortion | Damage is localized to a spray, heat, or mechanical event | Only old leaves are affected while new growth remains normal
lookAlikes: Calcium deficiency | Broad mite | Hemp russet mite | Herbicide or growth-regulator injury | Root disease
confirmation: Review fertilizer and source-water boron and measure root-zone pH/EC before assigning the cause. | Use representative tissue analysis when the diagnosis is consequential; the published Cannabis values are experiment-specific, not universal thresholds.
immediateActions: Preserve pre-correction root-zone and tissue measurements. | Inspect distorted growth under magnification for mites before changing nutrition.
correctivePlan: Correct a confirmed boron under-supply gradually with a crop-appropriate nutrition plan. | Track new meristem and root growth; damaged leaves and dead tips will not reverse.
prevention: Maintain complete micronutrient supply and calibrated root-zone monitoring. | Avoid diagnosing micronutrients from internet deficiency charts without measurements.
warnings: The controlled study used one cultivar and complete boron withholding. | Boron has a narrow adequacy-to-toxicity margin in many crops; do not add boron from visual suspicion alone.

name: Calcium deficiency
summary: A calcium-supply or transport disorder that can damage meristems, newly expanding leaves, roots, fan leaves, and sugar leaves. Controlled Cannabis studies produced different canopy-onset patterns, so spotting, curled tips, or marginal necrosis require feed, water, root-zone, tissue, stage, and cultivar evidence.
affectedParts: growing tips and newly expanding leaves in vegetative T1 | lower fan leaves at flowering-stage onset in Gelato 29 | upper fan leaves and sugar leaves as the Gelato 29 sequence advanced | leaflet bases, interveinal tissue, serrations, margins, and tips | root tips and root system | developing inflorescences and bracts for differential inspection
stages: vegetative growth | flowering | chronic insufficient supply or impaired transport
indicators: Vegetative T1: growing tips and new leaves become stunted and irregular while leaflet bases stay narrow and paler than tips | Vegetative T1 progression: basal yellowing intensifies into interveinal chlorosis, distorted new leaves, marginal necrosis, growing-tip death, and increased axillary branching | Flowering Gelato 29: lower fan leaves begin with interveinal yellow rings around necrotic brown centers during week three of withholding | Flowering Gelato 29 progression: spotting concentrates near margins and tips, coalesces into irregular marginal necrosis, and browns serration points | Later flowering progression: injury moves upward into younger fan and sugar leaves, with upward curling of upper fan-leaf tips | A calcium deficit or impaired calcium delivery is supported by input, root-zone, water, tissue, and plant-stage measurements linked to the imaged plant
exclusions: Spots, edge burn, or curl occur without a documented calcium-supply or transport problem | Root-zone EC is high and broad multi-ion salt injury explains the tip and margin damage | Roots are saturated, oxygen-limited, drought-stressed, temperature-injured, mechanically damaged, or diseased and calcium analysis does not support a deficit | Young-growth distortion is accompanied by mites, thrips, insects, webbing, eggs, fecal spots, or feeding scars | Discrete expanding lesions, halos, fungal structures, or laboratory results support a pathogen | Injury is limited to the hottest, brightest, sprayed, or contact-exposed canopy surfaces | Older-leaf marginal injury follows a potassium- or magnesium-type pattern and tissue/root-zone evidence supports that alternative | Yellowing is consistent with measured nitrogen deficiency or late-cycle senescence and no calcium evidence is present | Color or spotting is visible only under altered lighting, white balance, residue, dust, or compression artifact
lookAlikes: Potassium deficiency | Magnesium deficiency | Boron deficiency or toxicity | High-EC nutrient burn or salinity | Waterlogging or root-zone hypoxia | Drought or excessive vapor demand | Cold or overheated root zone | Pythium or other root disease | Broad mite injury | Hemp russet mite injury | Thrips feeding injury | Heat or high-light injury | Foliar spray phytotoxicity | Leaf-spot pathogen | Normal late-flower senescence
confirmation: Do not confirm calcium deficiency from rust-colored spots, curled leaf tips, distorted new growth, marginal necrosis, one photograph, or one video. | Capture serial whole-plant, growing-tip, upper/middle/lower-canopy, fan-leaf, sugar-leaf, leaf upper-surface, underside, cleaned-root, and root-tip views under repeatable lighting with scale and a matched same-cultivar plant. | Record the first affected node and leaf age, cultivar, stage, days since symptom onset, irrigation and dryback, root-zone water content, temperature, pH, EC, and dissolved oxygen where relevant. | Measure calcium and competing ions in source water, fertilizer stocks, final solution, root-zone extract, substrate or soil, and representative leaf tissue from defined upper and lower canopy positions. | Interpret tissue results using plant part, node, stage, cultivar, method, and system context; neither 0.39% from T1 nor the Gelato 29 upper/lower relationship is a universal threshold. | Inspect roots for active white tips, discoloration, softness, odor, lesions, binding, and mechanical damage; use a plant diagnostic laboratory when root pathogens or leaf lesions remain plausible. | Inspect distorted growth and both leaf surfaces with magnification for broad mites, russet mites, thrips, eggs, webbing, and feeding evidence. | Retain a suspected label until a calcium-supply or transport problem, compatible progression, and exclusion evidence are linked to the photographed plant.
immediateActions: Preserve pre-treatment images, nutrient labels, mixing records, solution and water samples, root-zone readings, and representative tissue before changing the program. | Verify meter calibration, formulation calculations, source-water mineral content, root health, pH, EC, water status, and temperature before adding calcium or flushing. | Remove symptom-only samples from training-ground-truth collections until analytical and exposure evidence is reviewed.
correctivePlan: Correct the verified supply, pH, salinity, irrigation, temperature, oxygen, drainage, or root-health cause using crop-, medium-, and stage-appropriate agronomic guidance. | Restore a balanced nutrient solution rather than stacking unmeasured calcium-magnesium products; account for calcium already present in source water and fertilizers. | Track new growth, new roots, lesion rate, root-zone pH and EC, and follow-up tissue results; reopen potassium, magnesium, boron, pest, pathogen, and environmental differentials if response is absent.
prevention: Test source water and complete fertilizer for calcium and competing ions and document all calcium-containing inputs. | Use calibrated root-zone pH, EC, moisture, temperature, and irrigation monitoring appropriate to the production system. | Maintain same-cultivar healthy references and consistent upper/lower canopy tissue-sampling and serial imaging procedures.
warnings: Controlled Cannabis studies disagreed on first affected canopy location: vegetative T1 began at growing tips and new leaves, while flowering Gelato 29 began on lower fan leaves; location alone is not ground truth. | The T1 five-week timing, 0.39% most-recent-mature-leaf value, and growing-tip sequence are experiment-specific. | The Gelato 29 three-week onset, upper/lower tissue relationship, and biomass response came from three deep-water-culture plants per treatment and must not be generalized. | Calcium can be present in the root zone while water status, salinity, temperature, oxygen, damaged roots, or transport conditions limit delivery; adding calcium does not correct those causes. | The CC BY figure is a single-treatment progression, but remains excluded from automated training until panel annotations, source grouping, and a leakage-safe dataset split are assigned. | The NC State e-GRO page requires author permission for its separate images; those assets were not copied or admitted. | All symptom-only samples remain low confidence and require human review.

name: Copper deficiency
summary: A controlled vegetative Cannabis copper-withholding response characterized by late-onset stunting, basal narrowing and yellowing of newer leaflets, progressive new-leaf distortion, fine interveinal chlorosis, slight inward/downward margin curl, and reduced turgidity. The evidence comes from one cultivar and requires tissue and root-zone confirmation.
affectedParts: whole plant for relative stunting | growing tips and newer foliage | newly expanding leaflets | leaflet bases | interveinal tissue | leaf margins | most-recent-mature leaves for source-comparable tissue analysis | roots and root zone for availability checks
stages: vegetative | late-onset deficiency | initial basal narrowing and yellowing | advanced distortion and fine interveinal chlorosis
indicators: Slight whole-plant stunting relative to a matched healthy plant | Newer and expanding leaves show mild distortion concentrated near leaflet bases | Leaflet bases become narrower than the distal leaflet and slightly yellow | Basal narrowing and distortion become more pronounced as the sequence advances | Marginal interveinal chlorosis develops on new and expanding leaves | Advanced leaves show fine interveinal chlorosis across much of the blade | Leaf margins distort and curl slightly inward and downward | New and expanding leaves show mildly reduced turgidity | Low copper is documented in correctly positioned foliage and linked to supply or root-zone availability
exclusions: New-leaf interveinal chlorosis occurs without basal narrowing or distortion and iron, manganese, or zinc evidence is stronger | Growing-tip distortion, narrow leaflet bases, root-tip loss, severe wilting, or tip death follows a boron-deficiency pattern and boron analysis supports it | Newest leaves are puckered, bronzed, hardened, or strap-like and broad mites are found under adequate magnification | Uniform wilting or reduced turgidity follows irrigation, drought, heat, root hypoxia, salinity, or root disease rather than the published leaf sequence | Fine stippling, silver scars, webbing, eggs, mites, thrips, or fecal spots are present on magnified inspection | Mosaic, vein clearing, brittle growth, asymmetrical distortion, or molecular evidence supports a virus or viroid | Discrete lesions, halos, surface growth, vascular discoloration, root decay, or laboratory evidence supports a pathogen | Damage maps to a lamp-facing surface, heat event, spray droplets, residue, rubbing point, pruning event, or other documented exposure | Color or distortion appears only under grow lights, altered white balance, glare, shadow, compression, residue, or a stable inherited leaf form | Correctly positioned tissue copper is adequate for the cultivar, stage, method, and production system or another nutrient result explains the syndrome better
lookAlikes: Iron deficiency | Manganese deficiency | Zinc deficiency or phosphorus-zinc interaction | Boron deficiency | Calcium deficiency | Broad mite injury | Hemp russet mite injury | Thrips injury | Virus or viroid syndrome | High-pH or high-EC root-zone stress | Waterlogging or root-zone hypoxia | Drought or excessive vapor demand | Pythium or other root disease | Heat or high-light injury | Foliar spray or plant-growth-regulator injury | Genetic or developmental leaf-shape variation | Camera white-balance, exposure, or grow-light color shift
confirmation: Do not confirm copper deficiency from stunting, narrow leaflet bases, chlorosis, curl, reduced turgidity, one photograph, or one video; retain a suspected label until analytical and root-zone evidence is linked to the photographed plant. | Capture serial whole-plant and matched upper-, middle-, and lower-canopy views, growing tips, new and mature leaves of known node and physiological age, leaflet bases and margins, both leaf surfaces, internodes with scale, and roots under neutral repeatable lighting with a healthy same-cultivar reference. | Record cultivar, stage, days since onset, copper concentration and formulation, iron, manganese, zinc, boron, calcium, sulfur, phosphorus, and complete fertilizer inputs, source-water chemistry and alkalinity, irrigation history, substrate or solution type, and recent product changes. | Measure root-zone pH, EC, water content, temperature, drainage, and oxygenation as appropriate to the system, and inspect washed roots before changing copper supply. | Submit correctly positioned foliage plus appropriate solution, substrate, soil, leachate, or water samples to an agricultural or plant diagnostic laboratory; interpret copper with plant part, stage, cultivar, method, and competing elements rather than treating 1.41 mg/kg as a universal cutoff. | Inspect growing points and both leaf surfaces with magnification and use a plant diagnostic laboratory when broad mites, russet mites, thrips, root disease, viruses, viroids, or other pathogens remain plausible. | Treat response of subsequent growth as supporting evidence only; improvement after correcting a documented cause does not retroactively make the original image ground-truth copper deficiency.
immediateActions: Mark affected and matched healthy plants; preserve pre-treatment serial images, fertilizer and irrigation records, root-zone measurements, and representative tissue before changing nutrition. | Correct documented pH, salinity, saturation, drought, temperature, oxygenation, or root-health problems before assuming copper concentration is inadequate. | Avoid blind copper supplementation when boron, iron, manganese, zinc, mites, pathogens, spray injury, and genetic leaf form have not been excluded.
correctivePlan: When analytical and production records support inadequate copper supply or availability and roots are functional, restore a balanced crop- and system-appropriate micronutrient program gradually under current local agronomic guidance. | Track subsequent leaf geometry, chlorosis, turgidity, internode growth, roots, root-zone measurements, and follow-up tissue results rather than judging correction from old deformed leaves. | If copper status is adequate or the pattern continues, reopen boron, iron, manganese, zinc, calcium, root disease, arthropod, pathogen, environmental, exposure, and genetic differentials.
prevention: Record copper and competing micronutrients in fertilizer, source water, and representative tissue by plant part and stage rather than relying on a generic deficiency chart. | Calibrate pH and EC meters, monitor root-zone conditions and leachate where appropriate, and keep irrigation, dryback, temperature, and oxygenation records. | Maintain same-cultivar healthy references and consistent growing-tip, node-, and canopy-position sampling so developmental leaf shape is not mistaken for copper response.
warnings: The controlled sequence came from one Cannabis sativa T1 cultivar in silica sand with copper completely withheld; nine weeks, 1.41 mg/kg tissue copper, 45% lower biomass, and the pictured pattern are experiment-specific, not universal thresholds. | The control contained 4.65 mg/kg copper, slightly below the general crop survey range cited by the authors, which further limits conversion of either value into a Cannabis cutoff. | The source contains a figure-number inconsistency: its copper prose cites Figure 5, while the published Figure 4 caption and right-column label identify copper deficiency and Figure 5 is captioned manganese and boron toxicity. Copper panels require human verification against the original layout. | New-growth distortion, basal narrowing, chlorosis, curl, reduced turgidity, and stunting overlap nutritional, root-zone, arthropod, pathogen, environmental, exposure, genetic, and imaging conditions and are not image-only ground truth. | The CC BY Figure 4 asset is already hashed and indexed under manganese deficiency; it is cross-referenced rather than duplicated here because repository quality gates require unique verified media hashes. | No separate image or video is admitted for this record in this batch; all symptom-only samples and any derived copper-panel crops require human review and linked analytical evidence before ground-truth use.

name: Iron deficiency
summary: A context-dependent iron-status disorder that produced upper-canopy, new-leaf interveinal chlorosis in a controlled vegetative T1 study, but no visible syndrome in a controlled flowering Gelato 29 study despite substantially lower foliar iron. Images can support a differential, but cannot confirm or exclude iron deficiency.
affectedParts: growing tip and newly expanding leaves | upper half of the canopy | leaflet margins and bases during the controlled early sequence | middle and lower foliage as distribution controls | roots and root zone for availability checks | whole plant for serial comparison
stages: vegetative evidence from a transplant-onward withholding experiment | flowering evidence from a symptom-negative 7.5-week withholding experiment
indicators: Slight marginal yellowing, especially near leaflet bases, was the first controlled-study sign | Interveinal chlorosis develops on new and expanding leaves while veins remain relatively greener | Paling spreads through the upper half and is most apparent at the growing tip | Middle and lower foliage can remain healthy dark green during the vegetative controlled-study sequence | Serial upper-canopy images show progression rather than a fixed camera, lighting, or exposure artifact | Low foliar iron can occur with no visible syndrome, so a normal-looking canopy does not exclude inadequate iron status
exclusions: Older leaves are affected first with sharply interveinal chlorosis, favoring magnesium rather than the controlled iron sequence | Uniform lower-leaf yellowing or normal late-flower fade explains the pattern better | Chlorosis maps only to the lamp-facing canopy, a hot spot, bleaching, or a recorded heat or light event | Fine stippling, silver scars, webbing, eggs, mites, thrips, or fecal spots are found on magnified inspection | Mosaic, distortion, vein clearing, stunting, or laboratory evidence supports a virus, viroid, or other pathogen | Damage maps to spray droplets, residue, rubbing points, or another documented contact exposure | A stable cultivar pattern or sector follows the same tissue boundaries without progressive chlorosis | Root decay, saturation, hypoxia, abnormal temperature, salinity, pH, or irrigation history explains impaired uptake | Appropriately sampled tissue and root-zone testing support manganese, zinc, sulfur, nitrogen, calcium, or another diagnosis more strongly
lookAlikes: Manganese deficiency | Zinc deficiency | Sulfur deficiency | Magnesium deficiency | Nitrogen deficiency or normal late-flower senescence | Calcium deficiency | High-pH or high-EC root-zone stress | Waterlogging, root-zone hypoxia, or root disease | Light bleaching or heat stress | Broad mite, spider mite, or thrips injury | Virus, viroid, or mosaic-like disorder | Spray, residue, or mechanical injury | Genetic variegation | Camera white-balance, exposure, or grow-light color shift
confirmation: Keep symptom-only image and video labels at low confidence: neither upper chlorosis nor a visually normal canopy confirms or excludes iron deficiency. | Capture serial whole-plant and matched upper-, middle-, and lower-canopy views, plus new and mature leaves on both surfaces, under neutral repeatable lighting with scale, leaf node, physiological age, and a healthy same-cultivar reference. | Record cultivar, stage, fertilizer iron concentration and chelate or formulation, source-water iron and alkalinity, irrigation history, substrate or solution type, and recent environmental or product changes. | Measure root-zone pH, EC, water content, temperature, drainage, and oxygenation as appropriate to the system, and inspect washed roots for decay or restricted growth before changing iron supply. | Submit correctly positioned leaf tissue and, where appropriate, solution, substrate, soil, or water samples to an agricultural or plant diagnostic laboratory; interpret iron and competing nutrients using crop-, organ-, stage-, and method-appropriate references. | Inspect both leaf surfaces and growing tips with magnification and use a plant diagnostic laboratory when arthropods, root disease, viruses, viroids, or other pathogens remain plausible. | Use subsequent new-leaf response only as supporting evidence; improvement after correcting an identified cause does not retroactively make the original image a ground-truth iron-deficiency sample.
immediateActions: Mark the plant and preserve pre-treatment serial images, feed and irrigation records, root-zone measurements, and representative tissue before changing nutrition. | Correct documented pH, salinity, saturation, temperature, oxygenation, or root-health problems before assuming the iron concentration is inadequate. | Avoid adding iron or changing chelates from color alone, especially when manganese, zinc, sulfur, pests, pathogens, or a lighting artifact have not been excluded.
correctivePlan: When analytical and production records support inadequate iron supply or availability and roots are functional, restore a balanced crop- and system-appropriate iron program gradually under current local agronomic guidance. | Track subsequent leaves, root growth, root-zone measurements, and follow-up tissue results; do not judge correction solely by old chlorotic leaves. | If iron status is adequate or the pattern continues, reopen manganese, zinc, sulfur, magnesium, root disease, arthropod, pathogen, light, heat, exposure, and genetic differentials.
prevention: Record the iron source, chelate or formulation, complete fertilizer composition, source-water chemistry, pH, EC, and irrigation conditions against plant and media identifiers. | Use routine same-position tissue sampling and production-system-appropriate root-zone or soil testing before visible injury. | Maintain healthy same-cultivar visual references and neutral-light serial imaging of upper, middle, and lower canopy positions.
warnings: The visible sequence came from one Cannabis sativa T1 cultivar grown in silica sand with iron withheld from transplant; nine weeks, 60.08 mg/kg tissue iron, and the pictured appearance are experiment-specific, not universal diagnostic thresholds. | A separate flowering study found no visible iron-deficiency symptoms in three Gelato 29 plants despite foliar iron below half the control value; symptom absence cannot rule out inadequate iron status, and this small experiment does not prove that flowering Cannabis never develops visible symptoms. | The controlled vegetative study found no significant biomass difference at the symptom-onset harvest, so visual severity must not be converted into a universal yield-loss estimate. | Upper interveinal chlorosis is shared by other nutritional, root-zone, biotic, environmental, genetic, and imaging conditions and is not image-only ground truth. | The CC BY figure contains both iron- and zinc-deficiency columns and three severity rows; it is excluded from automated training until panels are bounded, class- and stage-annotated, scientifically reviewed, and assigned a leakage-safe split. | All symptom-only and symptom-negative samples require human review and linked analytical evidence before ground-truth use.

name: Potassium deficiency
summary: A stage- and leaf-type-dependent potassium-status disorder. Controlled vegetative plants developed older-leaf serration and margin yellowing followed by inward tan necrosis, while flowering plants showed an earlier sugar-leaf lesion pathway and a later fan-leaf tip-and-margin pathway. Edge burn alone is nonspecific and requires analytical and root-zone confirmation.
affectedParts: lower and older foliage in the vegetative T1 sequence | saw-tooth serrations and leaflet margins | larger sugar leaves near flowering inflorescences | secondary branch veins within sugar leaves | lower fan-leaf tips and marginal teeth | middle-canopy fan leaves during flowering progression | interveinal fan-leaf tissue as browning expands inward | roots and root zone for availability checks
stages: vegetative | flowering | pre-symptomatic low-potassium exposure | initial leaf-type-specific symptoms | advanced canopy-wide browning and desiccation
indicators: Burned leaf edges | Rust or tan spotting | Weak stems | Older leaves affected first | Vegetative T1 plants begin with yellowing along lower and older leaflet margins, especially saw-tooth serrations | Vegetative marginal yellowing intensifies and advances inward toward the midrib before tan marginal necrosis develops | Flowering sugar leaves can develop dark-brown lesions surrounding secondary branch veins before fan-leaf symptoms appear | Flowering lower fan leaves develop lighter browning at leaflet tips and marginal teeth | By week five, sugar-leaf injury predominates near the top while fan-leaf injury is strongest in the middle third | Advanced fan-leaf browning extends inward through interveinal tissue and leaves become curled and dry | A widespread serial pattern affects many leaves and is linked to low potassium in correctly positioned tissue and nutrient or root-zone evidence
exclusions: Only leaf tips burned immediately after a high-EC feed or fertilizer event and broad multi-ion salinity explains the pattern | Injury is confined to the hottest or brightest canopy face and measured light or leaf temperature explains it | Marginal chlorosis and necrosis are paired with elevated tissue boron or a verified boron exposure source | Interveinal yellowing retains strongly green veins without a serration-first pattern and magnesium evidence is stronger | Uniform yellowing follows nitrogen deficiency, sulfur deficiency, or normal late-flower senescence more closely | Dark sugar-leaf lesions are discrete, expanding, water-soaked, haloed, or associated with fungal structures or a positive laboratory pathogen result | Fine stippling, silver scars, webbing, eggs, mites, thrips, chewing, frass, or fecal spots are present | Damage follows a foliar spray, residue, fan abrasion, trellis contact, pruning, or another documented local exposure | Roots are saturated, oxygen-limited, drought-stressed, temperature-injured, mechanically damaged, or diseased enough to explain impaired uptake | Color or edge contrast appears only under grow lights, altered white balance, glare, shadow, compression, residue, or stable cultivar pigmentation
lookAlikes: High-EC nutrient burn or salinity | Boron toxicity | Magnesium deficiency | Nitrogen deficiency | Sulfur deficiency | Normal late-flower senescence | Drought or excessive vapor demand | Waterlogging or root-zone hypoxia | High-pH or otherwise unsuitable root-zone pH | Cold or overheated root zone | Pythium or other root disease | Heat or high-light injury | Foliar spray phytotoxicity | Wind, fan, trellis, or contact abrasion | Leaf-spot or vascular pathogen | Spider mite, broad mite, hemp russet mite, or thrips injury | Virus or viroid syndrome | Cultivar pigmentation or camera color artifact
confirmation: Do not confirm potassium deficiency from leaf-edge burn, brown sugar-leaf lesions, rust color, one photograph, or one video; retain a suspected label until analytical and root-zone evidence is linked to the photographed plant. | Capture serial whole-plant and matched upper-, middle-, and lower-canopy views, large and small fan leaves of known node and physiological age, sugar leaves, inflorescences, leaf tips, margins, serrations, secondary veins, both leaf surfaces, and roots under neutral repeatable lighting with scale and a healthy same-cultivar reference. | Record cultivar, stage and flowering week, days since onset, potassium concentration and formulation, nitrogen, calcium, magnesium, sulfur, boron, and complete fertilizer inputs, source-water chemistry and alkalinity, irrigation history, and substrate or solution type. | Measure root-zone pH, EC, water content, temperature, drainage, and oxygenation as appropriate to the system, and inspect washed roots before changing potassium supply. | Submit strategically positioned fan- and sugar-leaf tissue plus appropriate solution, substrate, soil, leachate, or water samples to an agricultural or plant diagnostic laboratory; interpret potassium with plant part, stage, cultivar, method, salinity, and competing ions. | Inspect both leaf surfaces, lesions, and roots with magnification and use a plant diagnostic laboratory when arthropods, root disease, leaf-spot pathogens, viruses, viroids, or other infectious causes remain plausible. | Treat subsequent new-growth response as supporting evidence only; improvement after correcting a documented cause does not retroactively make the original image ground-truth potassium deficiency.
immediateActions: Mark affected and matched healthy plants; preserve pre-treatment serial images, fertilizer and irrigation records, root-zone measurements, and representative fan- and sugar-leaf tissue before changing nutrition. | Correct documented salinity, pH, saturation, drought, temperature, oxygenation, or root-health problems before assuming potassium concentration is inadequate. | Avoid blind potassium or bloom-booster additions when high EC, boron, magnesium, pests, pathogens, spray injury, heat, and senescence have not been excluded.
correctivePlan: When analytical and production records support inadequate potassium supply or availability and roots are functional, restore a balanced crop- and system-appropriate nutrient program gradually under current local agronomic guidance. | Track subsequent leaves by type, node, and canopy position; new-lesion rate; roots; root-zone measurements; and follow-up tissue results rather than judging correction from old burned margins. | If potassium status is adequate or the pattern continues, reopen salinity, boron, magnesium, nitrogen, sulfur, root disease, arthropod, pathogen, environmental, exposure, senescence, and genetic differentials.

name: Magnesium deficiency
summary: A stage- and canopy-dependent magnesium-status disorder characterized by interveinal chlorosis that retains greener veins and can progress to interveinal necrosis. Controlled vegetative plants began on older lower foliage, while a flowering trial shifted rapidly toward smaller, younger fan leaves; images require tissue and root-zone confirmation.

stages: vegetative | flowering | pre-symptomatic low-magnesium exposure | initial interveinal chlorosis | advanced chlorosis and interveinal necrosis

name: Nitrogen deficiency
summary: A mobile-nutrient shortage that usually begins as an even yellowing of older leaves before moving upward.
affectedParts: older leaves | whole plant
indicators: Older leaves yellow first | Whole plant pale | Lower leaves drop | Growth slows
exclusions: New growth is affected first | Yellowing is sharply interveinal | Root-zone EC is already high
lookAlikes: Normal late-flower fade | Overwatering or root hypoxia | Magnesium deficiency
confirmation: Check whether symptoms begin on the oldest leaves. | Review root-zone pH and EC before adding fertilizer.
immediateActions: Measure pH and EC/PPM before changing feed. | Correct watering or root-zone problems first.
correctivePlan: If EC is low and pH is in range, increase complete nutrition gradually. | Recheck new growth over 5–7 days.
prevention: Track input and runoff EC. | Avoid reducing nitrogen too early in flower.
warnings: Do not diagnose from one yellow leaf. | Do not add nitrogen when high EC or root damage is the primary cause.
